query: For the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets that are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain why their mechanical properties differ during deformation and failure when constituent count alone is inadequate? Specify a controlled comparison, predictions relative to the quinary baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Removal of Mn from the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy reduces magnetic frustration, thereby lowering the energy barrier for a deformation-induced fcc-to-hcp phase transformation that occurs locally at stacking faults and twin boundaries. This transformation enhances strain hardening and ductility in the Mn-removed (ternary or quaternary) alloys compared to the quinary baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase FCC structure achieved by thermomechanical processing
generation.intervention: Conduct a controlled comparative test between the CrMnFeCoNi (quinary) alloy and its Mn-removed derivatives (e.g., the CrCoNi ternary or a relevant quaternary alloy), subjecting both to identical deformation conditions.
generation.conditions: Uniaxial tensile (or equivalent) deformation tests performed at controlled strain rates and temperatures (e.g., room and cryogenic temperatures) to ensure that any observed differences arise from the intrinsic phase transformation behavior rather than extrinsic processing variables.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale hcp phase lamellae that form along dislocation-induced stacking faults and twin interfaces during deformation
generation.mechanism: In alloys without Mn, the absence of magnetically frustrated interactions allows a more favorable fcc-to-hcp transformation during deformation. This localized phase transformation acts as an additional mode of strain accommodation, thereby improving the balance between strength and ductility. In contrast, in the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, magnetic frustration from Mn suppresses this transformation, resulting in different mechanical responses.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical test conditions, the Mn-removed alloys (ternary/quaternary) will show a measurable increase in the formation of an hcp phase during deformation, leading to a higher strain hardening rate and increased ductility compared to the quinary CrMnFeCoNi baseline.
generation.boundary: All alloys are processed to be single-phase FCC and tested under consistent thermomechanical conditions (identical strain rates and temperatures) so that phase transformation kinetics are the primary variable.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative trend of enhanced hcp phase formation due to Mn removal is supported, the quantitative extent of the transformation and its exact impact on mechanical properties might vary with subtle processing differences and localized compositional inhomogeneities.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in-situ characterization (using synchrotron XRD or TEM) during deformation on both the quinary CrMnFeCoNi alloy and Mn-removed alloys (e.g., CrCoNi). Quantify the formation and distribution of the hcp phase along with full stress–strain measurements under identical testing conditions.
measurements: Stress–strain curves and work hardening rates
Phase fraction and spatial distribution of hcp and FCC phases via diffraction or electron microscopy
Magnetic configuration assessment via appropriate magnetic measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mn-removed alloys do not show a statistically significant increase in the deformation-induced hcp phase, or if their mechanical properties (e.g., strain hardening and ductility) are comparable to or inferior to those of the CrMnFeCoNi baseline under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that Mn removal triggers a beneficial fcc-to-hcp transformation mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractCrCoNi alloy exhibits a remarkable combination of strength and plastic deformation, even superior to the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy. We connect the magnetic and mechanical properties of CrCoNi, via a magnetically tunable phase transformation. While both alloys crystallize as single-phase face-centered-cubic (fcc) solid solutions, we find a distinctly lower-energy phase in CrCoNi alloy with a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure. Comparing the magnetic configurations of CrCoNi with those of other equiatomic ternary derivatives of CrMnFeCoNi confirms that magnetically frustrated Mn eliminates the fcc-hcp energy difference. This highlights the unique combination of chemistry and magnetic properties in CrCoNi, leading to a fcc-hcp phase transformation that occurs only in this alloy, and is triggered by dislocation slip and interaction with internal boundaries. This phase transformation sets CrCoNi apart from the parent quinary, and its other equiatomic ternary derivatives, and provides a new way for increasing strength without compromising plastic deformation. Medium entropy alloy CoCrNi has better mechanical properties than high entropy alloys such as CrMnFeCoNi, but why

Here we show that the origin of these extraordinary properties, in CrCoNi, is the existence of a nano-structured hcp phase, caused by metastability of the fcc phase at low temperatures. A remarkable aspect is that the hcp laths form only localized to stacking faults and twin interfaces, suggesting that an additional mode of strengthening in these alloys is operative. We then show that this mechanism is suppressed by magnetic frustration in CrMnFeCoNi and its other equiatomic ternary single-phase derivatives.

Figure 3c, d show the atomic magnetic moments for all calculations in fcc and hcp phases of the ternary and the quinary alloy, respectively. In the ternary alloy, clear patterns emerge for Ni and Co. Cr magnetic moment is mostly negative in the hcp phase but switches to positive values in some of the fcc configurations. The magnetic moments on Ni and Co in the quinary alloy show similar trends as in the ternary alloy, while Cr moments show a wider range of fluctuations. More importantly, Fe and Mn have more complicated trends; Mn moment switches between positive and negative values in both phases, and Fe appears to experience negative magnetic moments in the hcp structure. Pure Mn is an antiferromagnetic element. When combined with ferromagnetic elements Ni, Co and Fe and another antiferromagnetic element Cr, preferred antiparallel alignment of Mn spins cannot be completely satisfied. Pure Mn in fcc structure would be magnetically frustrated due to geometric constraints on nearest neighbor exchange interactions. In case of the HEA, the frustration also depends on composition, type and concentration of other elements. It is expected that frustration can be engineered by changing Mn

cited_evidence.text: We have shown the existence of a nanostructure with hcp phase in the equiatomic CrCoNi—an alloy widely considered to have a single-phase fcc structure. We observed a delineation between CrCoNi—with hcp as the ground state independent of the local atomic arrangements—and the CrCoMnFeNi HEA, where the magnetic frustration resulting from the addition of Mn breaks a clear trend for relative hcp vs fcc energies. In addition, we showed that there is no driving force for this phase transformation in any other equiatomic ternary derivatives of this HEA. These findings emphasize the fact that high-entropy alloys with more constituent elements are not necessarily superior to their derivatives. Instead, the combination of chemical and, as emphasized presently, magnetic identities of elements govern the properties. An important consequence of this finding is that new alloying combinations can be predicted based on similar favorable magnetic properties. These results provide a new paradigm for design of single-phase alloys with metastable structures through computational guidance and experimental validation.

chosen.approach: Magnetically tunable fcc–hcp transformation via Mn removal
